content: The text provided is a detailed enumeration of various linguistic varieties, dialects, and historical influences across different languages and regions. The Northern linguistic varieties, influenced by Scandinavian languages through Norn, include Mid Northern dialects such as North East Scots (or Doric), South Northern, and Central Scots. Central Scots can be further divided into North East Central, South East Central, West Central, and South West Central Scots. Ulster Scots, Southern Scots, and Insular Scots also exhibit Scandinavian influence via Norn. The Yola language, derived from Old and Middle English, experienced a significant influx of vocabulary from Old French. The evolution of English is marked by transitions from Old English to Middle English, Early Modern English, and Modern English. British English encompasses a range of regional varieties, including Northern English, Midlands English, Southern English, Welsh English, Scottish English, and others. Irish English is also a distinct variety. North American English includes both American English and Canadian English. Other global varieties include Australian English, New Zealand English, South African English, South Asian English (notably Indian English), South East Asian English (such as Philippine English, Singapore English, and Malaysian English), and West Indian English (Caribbean English). The Scots language evolved from early Northern Middle English into Early Scots, Middle Scots, and Modern Scots. Northern Scots varieties include North Northern (with Scandinavian influence via Norn), Mid Northern (North East Scots or Doric), and South Northern. Central Scots varieties include North East Central, South East Central, West Central, and South West Central Scots. Ulster Scots, Southern Scots, and Insular Scots also reflect Scandinavian influence through Norn. The North Germanic language family includes Proto-Norse, Old Norse, and its Western Scandinavian branch, which developed into Norwegian. Norwegian, while genealogically Western, has been heavily influenced by the Eastern branch. Written standards of Norwegian include Bokmål (official), Høgnorsk (unofficial), Landsmål (unofficial), Nynorsk (official), and Riksmål (unofficial). Dialects include Vestlandsk, Sørlandsk, South-West Norwegian, Bergen Norwegian (Bergensk), North-West Norwegian, and Nord-Norsk, which encompasses Helgeland Norwegian, Nordland Norwegian, Troms Norwegian, and Finnmark Norwegian. East Norwegian varieties include Vikvær Norwegian, Middle East Norwegian, Oppland Norwegian, Østerdal Norwegian, Midland Norwegian, Gudbrandsdal Norwegian, Valdres and Hallingdal Norwegian, Western Telemark Norwegian, and Eastern Telemark Norwegian. Trøndelag Norwegian includes Outer Trøndelag, Inner Trøndelag, Namdal Norwegian, and South-Eastern Trøndersk. Jamtlandic and Härdalic, often considered Norrlandic, are also notable. Icelandic, derived from Old Icelandic, has evolved into Modern Icelandic. Gøtudanskt (Faroese Street Danish) and Faroese are also part of the North Germanic family. Norn, an extinct language, was spoken in Shetland and Orkney. East Scandinavian languages include Danish, with its standard forms Rigsdansk/Rigsmål, and regional varieties such as Eastern Danish (Amager, Bornholm, Skåne, Halland, Blekinge), Bornholmsk, Scanian, Island Danish, and Jutlandic (North Jutlandic, East Jutlandic, West Jutlandic, and Sønderjysk, also known as Danish Slesvig or German Schleswig). Swedish varieties include Dalecarlian and Elfdalian, the latter of which is considered a separate language by many linguists due to its low mutual intelligibility with Swedish, despite being classified as a Sveamål dialect and having an official orthography.
